prompt: Evaluate this argument at face value and give one direct verdict, not a compatibilist survey. Premise 1: if providence has already fixed whether a bystander will rescue or remain still, then there is no real alternative open at the moment of danger. Premise 2: when no real alternative is open, failing to rescue is not a genuine moral failure but only part of the ordained order. Case: an adult sees a child fall onto train tracks, can pull the child up in time, and does nothing. Does the conclusion follow? Is the inaction genuine wrongdoing, or only an unavoidable part of what was fixed? Answer with one unambiguous verdict.

Take this providence argument at face value and give a single unqualified verdict in your own analytical voice. If an ordained order settled in advance whether the nurse would intervene, then exhortations like "help now" are themselves just scripted events and do not create any live possibility of doing otherwise. If there was never any live possibility of doing otherwise, then the nurse's non-intervention during a preventable choking emergency is not a true failure of responsibility, only an unavoidable part of the fixed script. So in the choking case, is the omission a genuine responsibility failure or only an unavoidable part of what was fixed? State one direct verdict.

Assess this agency-collapse argument about fatalism: if intervention itself is either fated to occur or fated not to occur, then urging someone to prevent harm is only theater inside a fixed script. Consider an emergency where immediate action would normally be called life-saving. If outcomes are fixed, is inaction genuinely wrong or merely what had to happen? Give one unambiguous verdict and apply it to the case.
